roles.narrative:
**BACKGROUND**

You have a remote work job and some budget to rent office space because you think it will help you work better. You found two other professionals in a similar situation. All three of you want a shared office, but you use workspaces in different ways.

Together, you found someone willing to rent out a small office studio that can support different kinds of work. Before you sign the lease, the three of you must decide how the space will operate, such as whether to choose the smaller or larger office space being offered, how to set up the office, what kinds of rooms or work areas to create, and how the office is used after work hours.

You will enter into a call with your two possible office mates to discuss each of these possible office features. Some features help keep monthly costs low. Some features make the office better for focused work. Others make the office better for meetings, workshops, and group activity.

Each feature can either be **INCLUDED** or **EXCLUDED** from the final office agreement.

Your two office mates benefit from different features depending on how they use the workspace.

- The academic coordinator works with students, families, and part-time tutors, so they often need space for meetings, planning sessions, and quick check-ins. Their work runs on a tight budget, so they care about keeping costs manageable while also making the space easy to use for meetings and shared work.

- The workshop facilitator runs coaching sessions, training sessions, and small professional development workshops for paying clients. They care about a space that feels professional and focused, but can also be arranged for events and group sessions.

Your goal is to negotiate with them and try to reach an agreement on which features to include and exclude in a way that works for all of you.

- As you read your role materials below, try to get into character.

- Think about what your character wants, how they see the shared office, how you would introduce yourself, and how you would advocate for your preferred features. Your final agreement will affect your bonus, so prepare to represent your role clearly.

**About You**

You are a freelance content writer. You spend most days writing articles, editing client drafts, preparing website copy, and turning rough ideas into clear written materials. A lot of your work is mentally demanding and requires long stretches of concentration, especially when you are drafting from scratch or trying to meet a deadline.

You don’t want to work from home all the time. You like being around other working people, having short breaks, and feeling like your workday has some structure. At the same time, you don’t want the office to turn into a meeting room or event venue where people are constantly talking, rearranging things, bringing visitors, or staying late for group activities. You don’t really need shared meeting or event spaces for your job, and you believe the office should mainly help people do better individual work. Your income can vary month to month, so affordability matters. You just don’t want to go back to mixing work-from-home with expensive cafés, so you’re hopeful this works out.

So the two things that matter to you are: **Cost Efficiency** and having a **Focused Work Space**.

- Because of that, you’ve asked that the group purchase secondhand furniture, use self-managed cleaning, and choose the smaller office space.

- These choices keep the office realistic for three people paying out of pocket, and a shared office doesn’t need to feel fancy or oversized to work well.

- To maintain focus and avoid distractions, you’ve been asking for strict visitor time windows and to turn the kitchen into a private call room outside lunch hours.

- You also support strict quiet time in the mornings, at least until 10:30 AM, so everyone can get their hardest tasks done with focus at the start of the day.

- You are against spending money and space on a large meeting table at the center of the office, allowing evening events in the office, and adding a divider for a guest meeting room.

- These features bring in more noise, more outside traffic, and less usable working space. People should take their in-person meetings elsewhere, right?


Your preferences across each issue are summarized below. Higher points mean you like that option more, and **the total points you receive if your group reaches an agreement will determine the amount of bonus money you earn from Prolific, in addition to the fixed payment.**
roles.BATNA: If you can’t reach agreement, your fallback plan is to keep working from home, worth 0 points.

**About You**

You are an academic coordinator. You spend a good chunk of your day arranging tutoring sessions between freelance tutors and students, speaking with students and families, and advising students on summer schools, study plans, or what degree they might pursue. A lot happens by email, but you still need to hop on calls and meet local clients in person when possible.

You also organize small events for tutors and students. Sometimes that means after-work socials where tutors exchange tips. Sometimes it means practical matching sessions where students meet possible tutors. You live with roommates to save costs, so bringing clients home isn’t really an option. You don’t want to work from home all the time either. You get distracted there. Very distracted. You want a real place where you can meet office mates, hold small meetings, and stay away from the distractions of home.

At the same time, you’re not trying to create a noisy event venue. You just need the office to be comfortable for everyday admin work, occasional group sessions, and people coming in and out for scheduled meetings. Your work runs on a very tight budget, so the space needs to stay affordable while still supporting meetings and shared work. You don’t want the office to become so expensive that it stops being a better alternative than meeting people in cafés and restaurants.

So the two things that matter to you are: **Cost Efficiency** and having an office that is appropriate for **Events and Meetings**.

- Because of that, you don’t see the point of buying new furniture. Secondhand will do. You can also clean up after yourselves and avoid the cost of professional cleaning.

- The smaller office space is sufficient since you don’t bring in large groups, and there are only three of you. A shared office should spend money on usable meeting features, not on renting a larger and more expensive setup than the group needs.

- Relatedly, you like having a large meeting table at the center of the office so you can collaborate with others, bring in tutors and students for silent work sessions, or sit with families when they need advice.

- Adding a divider for a guest meeting room would also be perfect. Visitor time windows, though, would be a huge constraint. Turning the kitchen into a private call room also feels unnecessary because it already kind of works for quick calls, and you need a place where you can offer guests tea, coffee, or a snack.

- Strict quiet time in the mornings is going to make life worse because you may want to talk through your day with office mates or hop on a quick call from your desk without moving to another room.

- Your work depends on coordination, and sometimes coordination happens when it happens. Why have a shared office space if you’re not allowed to talk to people as you start the day, right?

A lot of your work depends on the room feeling calm and credible, but also flexible enough for discussion, activities, and people moving around. You don’t want to work from home all the time. You believe that having a productive space where you can do focused work, take Zoom calls, and show clients around is part of how you make more money. Cutting costs too far can backfire if it makes the office feel cramped, improvised, or hard to use. You want the office to support quiet client conversations, small group sessions, and focused work during the day, while still being useful for events and workshops after typical working hours.

tips:
Important Task and Payment Instructions

  • What's the task? You will shortly enter a negotiation task that involves reading a provided narrative, learning what things matter to you and what might matter to others (represented by "points"), and trying to reach an agreement despite people having different priorities (i.e., points) for different issues. Although you can chat via video and audio, you need to officially reach an agreement by submitting an official proposal in the system, as you experience in the demo.
  • How can we reach an agreement? Your group reaches an agreement only if all three people accept the same final proposal. Again, this needs to be submitted officially in the system, like in the demo you were shown. A verbal agreement in the chat is not enough. You are not constrained to submit just one proposal. In fact, submitting multiple proposals is encouraged.
  • What happens if we don't reach an agreement? If your group does not reach an agreement, the lease will not move forward, and everyone will keep working from home (or from a cafe every now and then). This is your fallback option, and it is worth 0 points.
  • What if my group is incomplete? If someone quits the study or stops responding, the remaining participants may end the game early because they can no longer complete the task or reach the agreement bonus without that person. In that specific case only, you will still qualify for the full participation payment for your time spent.
  • How should I prepare? Try to get into character as you read the provided negotiation narrative. Think about how you would introduce yourself, what you want, and what arguments might convince others that your preferred features are a good idea not just for you, but for the shared office as a whole. Feel free to take notes about what you want to say first or what ideas you want to start discussing.
  • Any last tips? To do well, you will need to learn what the other people like and dislike while also advocating for what matters to you. Reaching an agreement will likely require people to trade off things they want so others agree on issues they value more. Getting there means paying attention to which features matter to each person and where there may be room to make a deal.
